meta.rendering_note: All mathematics is KaTeX inside \( ... \) delimiters, one unnested span per expression. Subscripted quantities such as \( v_e \), \( v_o \), \( g_h \) and \( g_d \) and the Greek-letter symbols \( \omega \) and \( \lambda \) are each a single KaTeX span; no raw Unicode math symbol or Greek letter appears anywhere in this file. Gravitational potential energy and the total energy of a bound circular orbit are always written with their negative sign (zero of potential energy at infinity), while escape velocity, orbital velocity, kinetic energy and g-values are always non-negative. Every numeric answer terminates cleanly or is given as a clean order of magnitude.

topics.name: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
topics.summary: Kepler's three laws describe how planets move. The law of orbits says every planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus (a circle is the special case where the foci coincide). The law of areas says the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, which is simply conservation of angular momentum for a central force; it forces the planet to move fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion. The law of periods says \( T^2 \propto a^3 \), so a planet at four times the distance takes eight times as long. Newton explained all three with the universal law of gravitation: any two point masses attract with \( F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2} \), directed along the line joining them, with \( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \) N m\(^2\) kg\(^{-2}\). The force is symmetric, so the Earth and Moon pull each other equally. For a uniform spherical shell the field is zero inside and behaves as if all mass sat at the centre outside (shell theorem). Equating gravity to the centripetal force for a circular orbit gives Kepler's third law directly.
key_formulas: \( F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2} \) (attractive, along the joining line)
\( T^2 \propto a^3 \), or \( T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r^3}{G M} \) for a circular orbit
Areal velocity \( \dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{L}{2m} \) is constant
\( v_p r_p = v_a r_a \) (angular momentum conservation on an ellipse)
topics.worked_example: Planet B orbits at four times the distance of planet A, whose period is 1 year. Kepler's third law gives \( \dfrac{T_B^2}{T_A^2} = 4^3 = 64 \), so \( T_B = 8 \) years. If instead the comparison were a comet whose aphelion distance is three times its perihelion distance, conservation of angular momentum \( v_p r_p = v_a r_a \) gives an aphelion speed one-third of the perihelion speed.
common_mistakes: Placing the Sun at the centre of the ellipse instead of at a focus
Writing \( T \propto r \) or \( T^2 \propto r^2 \) instead of \( T^2 \propto r^3 \)
Applying the mass factor without squaring the distance factor when both change
Thinking the heavier body exerts the larger force; gravitational forces form an equal action-reaction pair
Applying the point-mass inverse-square law inside a shell, where the field is actually zero

topics.name: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
topics.summary: On a planet's surface \( g = \dfrac{G M}{R^2} \); it does not depend on the falling body's mass. Two very different formulas describe how \( g \) changes as you leave the surface. Going up, the inverse-square law gives \( g_h = g\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^2 \), which for small heights (\( h \ll R \)) is approximately \( g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) \): a linear-looking decrease with a factor 2, but \( g \) never reaches zero at any finite height. Going down, only the mass inside your radius attracts, and \( g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right) \) exactly, with no factor 2, reaching zero at the centre. So an equal reduction needs a depth twice the height. Inside the Earth \( g \) rises linearly from zero at the centre to its maximum at the surface, then falls as \( \dfrac{1}{r^2} \) outside. The Earth's rotation also matters: at latitude \( \lambda \), \( g' = g - R\omega^2\cos^2\lambda \), so the reduction is largest at the equator and zero at the poles, making \( g \) greatest at the poles. At fixed density \( g \propto R \).
key_formulas: \( g = \dfrac{G M}{R^2} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi G \rho R \)
\( g_h = g\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^2 \approx g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) \) for \( h \ll R \)
\( g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right) \) (exact, zero at the centre)
\( g' = g - R\omega^2\cos^2\lambda \) at latitude \( \lambda \)
Weightlessness at the equator when \( \omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}} \)
topics.worked_example: Take \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( R = 6400 \) km. At a height of 32 km, \( \dfrac{2h}{R} = 0.01 \), so \( g_h \approx 9.9 \) m/s\(^2\). At a depth of 64 km, \( \dfrac{d}{R} = 0.01 \), so \( g_d = 9.9 \) m/s\(^2\) as well: the same reduction needs twice the depth. At a height of \( \dfrac{R}{2} \) the linear formula fails; the exact result is \( g\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 = \dfrac{4g}{9} \).
common_mistakes: Using the depth formula \( 1 - d/R \) for a height, or the height formula \( 1 - 2h/R \) for a depth
Claiming \( g \) becomes zero at some finite height; it only tends to zero at infinity
Using the linear height approximation when \( h \) is comparable to \( R \)
Dropping the \( \cos^2\lambda \) factor, using \( \sin\lambda \), or forgetting to square the cosine
Saying \( g \) is smallest at the poles; it is largest there and smallest at the equator

topics.name: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
topics.summary: With the zero of potential energy at infinity, the gravitational potential energy of a mass \( m \) at distance \( r \) from the Earth's centre is \( U = -\dfrac{G M m}{r} \), negative at every finite distance. As a body falls inward \( U \) becomes more negative (decreases); as it rises \( U \) increases toward zero. The potential (energy per unit mass) is \( V = -\dfrac{G M}{r} \), which equals \( -gR \) at the surface. The change in potential energy from the surface to height \( h \) is \( \dfrac{m g h R}{R + h} \), which reduces to \( mgh \) only when \( h \ll R \). Escape velocity is the launch speed at which the total energy just reaches zero: \( \dfrac{1}{2} m v_e^2 = \dfrac{G M m}{R} \) gives \( v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 G M}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR} \), about 11.2 km/s for the Earth (using \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( R = 6400 \) km it comes out as exactly \( 8\sqrt2 \) km/s). It depends only on the planet's mass and radius, never on the projectile's mass or launch direction, and equals \( \sqrt2 \) times the orbital velocity at the same radius.
key_formulas: \( U = -\dfrac{G M m}{r} \), \( V = -\dfrac{G M}{r} \) (zero at infinity)
\( \Delta U = \dfrac{m g h R}{R + h} \) from the surface to height \( h \); \( \approx mgh \) for \( h \ll R \)
\( v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 G M}{R}} = \sqrt{2 g R} \)
Escape kinetic energy \( = \dfrac{G M m}{R} = m g R \)
Speed far away: \( v_{\infty}^2 = v^2 - v_e^2 \)
topics.worked_example: A body is launched vertically at half the escape velocity. Its kinetic energy is one-fourth of the escape energy, i.e. \( \dfrac{1}{4} m g R \). Setting this equal to \( \dfrac{m g h R}{R + h} \) gives \( \dfrac{h}{R+h} = \dfrac{1}{4} \), so \( h = \dfrac{R}{3} \). Using \( mgh \) instead would wrongly give \( \dfrac{R}{4} \).
common_mistakes: Dropping the negative sign of gravitational potential energy
Saying potential energy decreases as a body moves away; it increases (becomes less negative)
Using \( v_e = 2 v_o \) instead of \( v_e = \sqrt2\, v_o \)
Believing escape velocity depends on the projectile's mass or on the launch direction
Using \( mgh \) for heights comparable to \( R \)

topics.name: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
topics.summary: A satellite stays in a circular orbit because gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force: \( \dfrac{G M m}{r^2} = \dfrac{m v^2}{r} \). This gives the orbital velocity \( v_o = \sqrt{\dfrac{G M}{r}} \), which near the surface is \( \sqrt{gR} \), 8 km/s for the Earth; it does not depend on the satellite's mass and it falls as \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt r} \). The period is \( T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v_o} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{G M}} \) (Kepler's third law), about 84 minutes for a surface-skimming orbit. The energies have fixed relationships: \( KE = \dfrac{G M m}{2r} \), \( PE = -\dfrac{G M m}{r} \), so \( E = KE + PE = -\dfrac{G M m}{2r} = -KE = \dfrac{1}{2}PE \). The total energy is negative for every bound orbit; the binding energy \( +\dfrac{G M m}{2r} \) is the positive energy needed to remove the satellite to infinity and equals its kinetic energy. Escape from any radius needs \( \sqrt2 \) times the circular speed there, or twice the kinetic energy. A satellite that loses energy to friction spirals inward and actually speeds up.
key_formulas: \( v_o = \sqrt{\dfrac{G M}{r}} \); near the surface \( v_o = \sqrt{gR} \)
\( T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{G M}} \); near the surface \( T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}} \)
\( KE = \dfrac{G M m}{2r} \), \( PE = -\dfrac{G M m}{r} \), \( E = -\dfrac{G M m}{2r} \)
\( E = -KE = \dfrac{1}{2}PE \); binding energy \( = +\dfrac{G M m}{2r} \)
Launch energy from the surface to orbit radius \( r \): \( m g R - \dfrac{m g R^2}{2r} \)
topics.worked_example: A 100 kg satellite orbits at \( r = 2R \) with \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \) m. Using \( G M = g R^2 \): \( E = -\dfrac{m g R}{4} = -1.6 \times 10^9 \) J, \( KE = +1.6 \times 10^9 \) J and \( PE = -3.2 \times 10^9 \) J. The energy needed to launch it from rest on the surface is \( -1.6 \times 10^9 - (-6.4 \times 10^9) = 4.8 \times 10^9 \) J, i.e. \( \dfrac{3}{4} m g R \).
common_mistakes: Writing the total energy as positive by dropping the sign of the potential energy
Treating the binding energy and the total energy as the same number without flipping the sign
Using \( v \propto 1/r \) instead of \( 1/\sqrt r \), or \( T \propto r \) instead of \( r^{3/2} \)
Thinking a heavier satellite orbits more slowly; speed and period are independent of its mass
Assuming a satellite that loses energy slows down; it moves to a smaller orbit and speeds up

topics.name: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
topics.summary: A geostationary satellite has a period of exactly 24 hours, moves west to east in the equatorial plane and so stays above one fixed point on the equator; Kepler's third law puts it at a radius of about 42,000 km (about 6.6 Earth radii, a height of about 36,000 km), where its speed is only about 3 km/s. It cannot hover above any place off the equator, because every orbital plane must pass through the Earth's centre. A polar satellite instead circles at a low altitude (500 to 800 km) over both poles with a period of about 100 minutes; its orbital plane stays fixed while the Earth turns beneath it, so in about 14 passes per day it scans the whole globe. Weightlessness in orbit does not mean gravity is absent: the satellite and the astronaut fall freely together with the same acceleration, so the normal reaction, and therefore the apparent weight, is zero while gravity and the (negative) potential energy remain. The same idea gives the apparent weight in a lift, \( N = m(g + a) \) for upward acceleration and \( m(g - a) \) for downward, and zero in free fall. Kepler's third law \( T^2 \propto r^3 \) links any two orbits about the Earth.
key_formulas: Geostationary: \( T = 24 \) h, equatorial plane, \( r \approx 42000 \) km, height \( \approx 36000 \) km
\( \dfrac{T_1^2}{T_2^2} = \dfrac{r_1^3}{r_2^3} \) for any two orbits about the same body
Apparent weight: \( N = m(g + a) \) accelerating up, \( N = m(g - a) \) accelerating down, \( N = 0 \) in free fall
Gravitational force in orbit at distance \( r \): \( \dfrac{m g R^2}{r^2} \), not zero
Polar satellite: period \( \approx 100 \) min, about 14 orbits per day
topics.worked_example: A 70 kg astronaut orbits at \( r = 2R \) with \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\). The true gravitational force on him is \( 70 \times \dfrac{10}{4} = 175 \) N, yet his apparent weight is zero because he is in free fall with the satellite. Separately, if his apparent weight in a lift is 1.5 times his true weight, then \( g + a = 15 \), so the lift accelerates upward at 5 m/s\(^2\).
common_mistakes: Believing gravity is zero in orbit; weightlessness is the free-fall condition, not the absence of gravity
Thinking a geostationary satellite can be placed above a city off the equator
Confusing the geostationary height (36,000 km) with its orbital radius (42,000 km)
Applying the period ratio directly as the radius ratio instead of using \( T^2 \propto r^3 \)
Adding \( ma \) for a downward-accelerating lift, or subtracting it for an upward one

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: According to Kepler's first law, the orbit of a planet around the Sun is
options: an ellipse with the Sun at one of its foci
a circle with the Sun at its centre
an ellipse with the Sun at its centre
a parabola with the Sun at its focus
questions.explanation:
Kepler's first law (the law of orbits) states that every planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun located at one focus of the ellipse.

A circle is only a special case of an ellipse in which the two foci coincide, and even then the Sun sits at the focus, which is the centre only for that special case.

A parabola is an open curve, so it cannot describe a repeating planetary orbit.
questions.hint: Think about where the Sun sits inside the ellipse: at the middle, or at a special point off-centre?
distractor_logic: Assumes planetary orbits are exactly circular, which is only the special case of an ellipse with coinciding foci
Places the Sun at the geometric centre of the ellipse instead of at one focus
Uses a parabola, which is an open (unbound) path and cannot represent a repeating orbit

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: Kepler's second law states that the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. A direct consequence is that a planet
options: moves slowest when it is closest to the Sun
moves fastest when it is closest to the Sun
moves with the same speed at every point of its orbit
has a speed that does not depend on its distance from the Sun
questions.explanation:
For a given short time interval, the area swept is roughly a thin triangle of base \( r \) and height equal to the arc length \( v\,\Delta t \).

For the swept area to stay the same, a smaller \( r \) (closer to the Sun, at perihelion) must be compensated by a larger \( v \).

So the planet is fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion.
questions.hint: Equal areas in equal times: if the radius gets shorter, what must happen to the arc length covered?
distractor_logic: Reverses the conclusion: at smaller distance the arc must be longer, so the speed is greater, not smaller
Constant speed would sweep unequal areas since the radius changes along an ellipse
Speed clearly depends on distance, otherwise the equal-area rule could not hold on an ellipse

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: Kepler's third law relates the time period \( T \) of a planet to the semi-major axis \( a \) (or radius \( r \) for a circular orbit) of its orbit as
questions.explanation:
Kepler's third law (the law of periods) states that the square of the time period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis: \( T^2 \propto a^3 \).

For a circular orbit \( a = r \), so \( T^2 \propto r^3 \).

This follows from equating the gravitational force to the centripetal force for a circular orbit.
questions.hint: Squares on one side, cubes on the other: which quantity gets the cube?
distractor_logic: A linear relation would give the same speed at every radius, which contradicts orbital dynamics
\( T^2 \propto r^2 \) is just \( T \propto r \) in disguise and is not Kepler's law
Swaps the exponents: it is the period that is squared and the radius that is cubed

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: Two point masses \( m_1 \) and \( m_2 \) are separated by a distance \( r \). According to Newton's law of gravitation, the magnitude of the force between them is
questions.explanation:
Newton's universal law of gravitation: the force is directly proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

\( F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2} \), where \( G \) is the universal gravitational constant.

The force acts along the line joining the two masses and is always attractive.
questions.hint: Product of masses in the numerator, and the distance is squared in the denominator.
distractor_logic: Uses an inverse-first-power distance dependence instead of inverse-square
Adds the masses instead of multiplying them
Puts \( r^2 \) in the numerator, which would make the force grow with separation

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: The gravitational force between two bodies is \( F \). If the distance between them is doubled (masses unchanged), the new force is
questions.explanation:
\( F \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2} \).

Doubling \( r \) makes \( r^2 \) four times larger, so the force becomes one-fourth.

New force \( = \dfrac{F}{4} \).
questions.hint: Inverse square: doubling the distance multiplies the denominator by how much?
distractor_logic: Treats the force as inversely proportional to \( r \) rather than \( r^2 \)
Makes the force increase with distance, the opposite of attraction weakening with separation
Correct factor of 4 but in the wrong direction; the force decreases, not increases

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: The gravitational force between two bodies is \( F \). If both masses are doubled while the separation is kept the same, the force becomes
questions.explanation:
\( F \propto m_1 m_2 \).

Doubling each mass multiplies the product \( m_1 m_2 \) by \( 2 \times 2 = 4 \).

New force \( = 4F \).
questions.hint: The force depends on the product of the masses, not on their sum.
distractor_logic: Doubles only once, as if only one of the two masses had been doubled
Assumes the force does not depend on the masses at all
Cubes the factor as though three quantities had been doubled

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: The SI unit of the universal gravitational constant \( G \) is
questions.explanation:
From \( F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2} \), we get \( G = \dfrac{F r^2}{m_1 m_2} \).

Substituting units: \( G \) has units of N m\(^2\) kg\(^{-2}\).

Its accepted value is \( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \) N m\(^2\) kg\(^{-2}\).
questions.hint: Rearrange the force law to make \( G \) the subject and read off the units.
distractor_logic: Forgets that the distance appears squared in the force law
Swaps the roles of mass and distance in the unit expression
Puts kg in the numerator instead of the denominator

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: Two bodies of mass 10 kg each are kept 1 m apart. Taking \( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \) N m\(^2\) kg\(^{-2}\), the gravitational force between them is
questions.explanation:
\( F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2} = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 10 \times 10}{1^2} \).

\( F = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 100 = 6.67 \times 10^{-9} \) N.

This tiny value shows why gravitational attraction between everyday objects is never noticed.
questions.hint: Multiply \( G \) by the product of the masses; \( r = 1 \) m makes the denominator 1.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by only one of the two 10 kg masses
Adds the masses (giving 20) instead of multiplying them (giving 100)
Ignores the masses entirely and just quotes \( G \)

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of a planet of mass \( M \) and radius \( R \) is given by
questions.explanation:
A body of mass \( m \) on the surface experiences the force \( F = \dfrac{G M m}{R^2} \).

Its acceleration is \( g = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{G M}{R^2} \).

Note that \( g \) does not depend on the mass of the falling body.
questions.hint: Divide the gravitational force on a test mass by that test mass.
distractor_logic: Drops the square on \( R \); this is the form of the potential, not the field
Squares the planet's mass, which does not appear in the force law that way
Puts \( R \) in the numerator, making gravity stronger for larger planets of the same mass

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: As one goes to greater heights above the Earth's surface, the value of \( g \)
questions.explanation:
At height \( h \), \( g_h = \dfrac{G M}{(R + h)^2} \).

As \( h \) increases the denominator grows, so \( g_h \) decreases continuously.

It approaches zero only as \( h \) tends to infinity, never at any finite height.
questions.hint: Look at what happens to the distance from the Earth's centre in the inverse-square law.
distractor_logic: Reverses the trend; distance from the centre grows, so the field weakens
Treats \( g \) as a fixed universal constant, which it is not
Describes the behaviour inside the Earth going outward, not above the surface

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: The acceleration due to gravity at the centre of the Earth (assumed a uniform solid sphere) is
options: equal to \( g \), its surface value
questions.explanation:
Inside a uniform sphere, only the mass within radius \( r \) contributes to the field (shell theorem), giving \( g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right) \).

At the centre \( d = R \), so \( g_d = 0 \).

Physically, the pull from every direction cancels out exactly.
questions.hint: At the centre, how much mass lies inside your radius, and what does the pull from all sides add up to?
distractor_logic: Assumes \( g \) is the same everywhere inside the Earth
Applies the outside inverse-square formula at \( r = 0 \), which is invalid inside the Earth
This is the value at depth \( \dfrac{R}{2} \), not at the centre

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: At a small height \( h \) above the Earth's surface (\( h \ll R \)), the acceleration due to gravity is approximately
questions.explanation:
\( g_h = \dfrac{G M}{(R+h)^2} = g\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^{-2} \).

For \( h \ll R \), the binomial approximation gives \( g_h \approx g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) \).

The factor 2 comes from the square in the inverse-square law.
questions.hint: Expand \( (1 + x)^{-2} \) for small \( x \); what is the coefficient of \( x \)?
distractor_logic: This is the exact depth formula, wrongly applied to a height
Has the wrong sign, making \( g \) increase with height
Halves the coefficient instead of doubling it

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: At a depth \( d \) below the Earth's surface (Earth taken as a uniform sphere of radius \( R \)), the acceleration due to gravity is
questions.explanation:
At depth \( d \), only the inner sphere of radius \( R - d \) attracts. Its mass is \( M\dfrac{(R-d)^3}{R^3} \).

\( g_d = \dfrac{G}{(R-d)^2} \cdot M\dfrac{(R-d)^3}{R^3} = g\,\dfrac{R - d}{R} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right) \).

This is exact, not an approximation, and gives zero at the centre.
questions.hint: Only the mass inside your radius pulls you; that mass scales as the cube of the radius.
distractor_logic: Borrows the factor 2 from the small-height approximation, which does not apply inside the Earth
Has the wrong sign; \( g \) decreases as you go deeper
Invents a quadratic dependence; the inside variation is exactly linear

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: On the Earth's surface, the value of \( g \) is maximum at
questions.explanation:
The Earth's rotation reduces effective gravity by \( R \omega^2 \cos^2 \lambda \), which is largest at the equator (\( \lambda = 0^\circ \)) and zero at the poles (\( \lambda = 90^\circ \)).

The Earth is also slightly flattened, so the polar radius is smaller, which further increases \( g \) at the poles.

Hence \( g \) is maximum at the poles and minimum at the equator.
questions.hint: Where is the centripetal effect of Earth's spin the smallest?
distractor_logic: The equator is where rotation reduces \( g \) the most, so \( g \) is minimum there
At \( 45^\circ \) the reduction is half of the equatorial value, so it is intermediate
Ignores both the rotation effect and the Earth's flattening

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) at the surface and \( R = 6400 \) km, the acceleration due to gravity at a height of 32 km above the surface is approximately
questions.explanation:
Since \( h = 32 \) km is much smaller than \( R = 6400 \) km, use \( g_h \approx g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) \).

\( \dfrac{2h}{R} = \dfrac{64}{6400} = 0.01 \).

\( g_h \approx 10 \times 0.99 = 9.9 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Use the small-height formula; remember the factor 2.
distractor_logic: Uses the depth formula \( 1 - h/R \), dropping the factor 2
Adds instead of subtracts, making gravity stronger at height
Doubles the reduction again, as if using \( 4h/R \)

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) at the surface and \( R = 6400 \) km, the acceleration due to gravity at a depth of 128 km below the surface is
questions.explanation:
Inside the Earth, \( g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right) \), with no factor 2.

\( \dfrac{d}{R} = \dfrac{128}{6400} = 0.02 \).

\( g_d = 10 \times 0.98 = 9.8 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: The depth formula has no factor 2 in it.
distractor_logic: Applies the height formula with its factor 2 to a depth
Adds instead of subtracts; gravity decreases going inward
Halves the fractional depth without justification

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: Taking the zero of gravitational potential energy at infinity, the gravitational potential energy of a body of mass \( m \) at a finite distance \( r \) from the Earth's centre is
options: negative near the Earth but positive far away
questions.explanation:
With \( U = 0 \) at infinity, bringing a mass closer to the Earth means gravity does positive work on it, so its potential energy decreases below zero.

\( U = -\dfrac{G M m}{r} \), which is negative for every finite \( r \).

It approaches zero from below only as \( r \) tends to infinity.
questions.hint: Gravity does positive work as the body comes in from infinity; what does that do to \( U \)?
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign; \( U \) is below the reference value of zero everywhere
The zero is at infinity, not at the surface, so surface \( U \) is a large negative number
\( U \) is negative at every finite distance and only tends to zero far away

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: Due to the Earth's rotation with angular velocity \( \omega \), the effective acceleration due to gravity at the equator is less than that at the poles by
questions.explanation:
At latitude \( \lambda \), \( g' = g - R \omega^2 \cos^2 \lambda \).

At the equator \( \lambda = 0^\circ \) and \( \cos^2 \lambda = 1 \), so the reduction is \( R \omega^2 \).

At the poles \( \lambda = 90^\circ \) and the reduction is zero.
questions.hint: Centripetal acceleration of a point on the equator is \( \omega^2 R \).
distractor_logic: This is the reduction at \( 45^\circ \) latitude, where \( \cos^2 \lambda = 1/2 \)
Wrong powers: centripetal acceleration is \( \omega^2 R \), not \( \omega R^2 \)
Ignores the rotation effect altogether

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: If the Earth suddenly stopped rotating about its axis, the effective value of \( g \) at the equator would
questions.explanation:
Rotation reduces the effective gravity at the equator by \( R \omega^2 \), because part of the true gravitational pull provides the centripetal acceleration.

If rotation stopped, this reduction would vanish, so the effective \( g \) would rise by \( R \omega^2 \) to the true value \( \dfrac{G M}{R^2} \).
questions.hint: Rotation currently subtracts something from \( g \) at the equator; remove the subtraction.
distractor_logic: Reverses the direction of the effect; rotation reduces \( g \), so stopping it restores the full value
Ignores that rotation currently affects \( g \) at the equator
Confuses this with the situation where rotation is so fast that objects float

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: Take the rotational term \( R \omega^2 = 0.034 \) m/s\(^2\) for the Earth. The reduction in the effective value of \( g \) at a latitude of \( 60^\circ \), compared with the poles, is
questions.explanation:
Reduction \( = R \omega^2 \cos^2 \lambda \).

At \( 60^\circ \), \( \cos \lambda = \dfrac{1}{2} \), so \( \cos^2 \lambda = \dfrac{1}{4} \).

Reduction \( = 0.034 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.0085 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Square the cosine of the latitude before multiplying.
distractor_logic: Drops the \( \cos^2 \lambda \) factor entirely and uses the equatorial value
Uses \( \sin^2 \lambda = 3/4 \) instead of \( \cos^2 \lambda \)
Uses \( \cos \lambda = 1/2 \) without squaring it

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: The change in gravitational potential energy when a body of mass \( m \) is raised from the Earth's surface to a height \( h \) (not necessarily small compared with \( R \)) is
questions.explanation:
\( \Delta U = -\dfrac{G M m}{R + h} - \left(-\dfrac{G M m}{R}\right) = G M m\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R+h}\right) = \dfrac{G M m h}{R(R+h)} \).

Using \( G M = g R^2 \): \( \Delta U = \dfrac{m g h R}{R + h} \).

For \( h \ll R \) this reduces to the familiar \( m g h \).
questions.hint: Subtract the two \( -GMm/r \) values and simplify using \( GM = gR^2 \).
distractor_logic: This is only the small-height approximation; it over-estimates the true change for large \( h \)
Simplifies to \( m g R \), which is independent of \( h \) and is the energy to reach infinity, not height \( h \)
Has \( h \) alone in the denominator, giving infinite energy for tiny heights

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: The escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s. A planet has twice the mass and twice the radius of the Earth. The escape velocity from that planet is
questions.explanation:
\( v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 G M}{R}} \), so \( v_e \propto \sqrt{\dfrac{M}{R}} \).

With \( M \) and \( R \) both doubled, \( \dfrac{M}{R} \) is unchanged.

The escape velocity stays 11.2 km/s.
questions.hint: Only the ratio \( M/R \) matters.
distractor_logic: Doubles \( v_e \) as if only the mass had doubled and the radius were squared
Halves \( v_e \), as if only the radius change mattered
Multiplies by \( \sqrt2 \), as if only the mass had doubled

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \) m, the gravitational potential energy of a 100 kg body on the Earth's surface (zero at infinity) is
questions.explanation:
\( U = -\dfrac{G M m}{R} = -m g R \), using \( G M = g R^2 \).

\( U = -100 \times 10 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 = -6.4 \times 10^9 \) J.
questions.hint: Replace \( GM/R \) with \( gR \) and keep the negative sign.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign; surface potential energy is below the zero at infinity
Halves the value, confusing \( m g R \) with the orbital kinetic energy \( m g R / 2 \)
Uses \( R \) in km while keeping other quantities in SI units

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \) m, the minimum work required to move a 100 kg body from the Earth's surface to infinity is
questions.explanation:
Work needed \( = U_{\infty} - U_{surface} = 0 - \left(-m g R\right) = m g R \).

\( W = 100 \times 10 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 = 6.4 \times 10^9 \) J.

This positive work exactly cancels the negative binding energy at the surface.
questions.hint: Work done by you equals the increase in potential energy, from \( -mgR \) up to zero.
distractor_logic: Gives the potential energy at the surface rather than the (positive) work needed to leave it
Halves the value, confusing it with the orbital kinetic energy near the surface
Assumes the body is already free; it is bound and needs energy to escape

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: The escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s. For a planet of the same radius as the Earth but four times its mass, the escape velocity is
questions.explanation:
\( v_e \propto \sqrt{M} \) for fixed \( R \).

Four times the mass gives \( \sqrt4 = 2 \) times the escape velocity.

\( v_e = 2 \times 11.2 = 22.4 \) km/s.
questions.hint: Escape velocity goes as the square root of the mass.
distractor_logic: Scales linearly with mass instead of with its square root
Assumes escape velocity depends on radius only
Divides instead of multiplies

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: The minimum kinetic energy that must be given to a body of mass \( m \) on the surface of a planet (mass \( M \), radius \( R \)) so that it escapes is
questions.explanation:
At the surface \( U = -\dfrac{G M m}{R} \). To reach infinity with zero speed the total energy must become zero.

Required KE \( = 0 - U = \dfrac{G M m}{R} \).

This equals \( \dfrac{1}{2} m v_e^2 \), consistent with \( v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R} \).
questions.hint: The kinetic energy must exactly cancel the negative potential energy.
distractor_logic: This is the kinetic energy of a satellite orbiting just above the surface, half of what escape needs
Doubles the required value, as if escape needed twice the binding energy
Has the dimensions of force, not energy

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: A body is released from rest at a very large distance from the Earth (effectively infinity) and falls freely. Neglecting air resistance, its speed on reaching the Earth's surface is
questions.explanation:
Energy conservation: \( 0 + 0 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 - \dfrac{G M m}{R} \).

\( v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 G M}{R}} = \sqrt{2 g R} \).

This is exactly the escape velocity, as it must be by time-reversal symmetry.
questions.hint: Falling in from infinity is escape run backwards.
distractor_logic: This is the orbital velocity, which is \( \sqrt2 \) times smaller
Missing the square root; wrong dimensions
Halves the energy instead of doubling it

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: On the Moon, \( g = 1.6 \) m/s\(^2\) and the radius is \( 1.8 \times 10^6 \) m. The escape velocity from the Moon's surface is
questions.explanation:
\( v_e = \sqrt{2 g R} = \sqrt{2 \times 1.6 \times 1.8 \times 10^6} = \sqrt{5.76 \times 10^6} \) m/s.

\( v_e = 2.4 \times 10^3 \) m/s \( = 2.4 \) km/s.

This is much smaller than the Earth's 11.2 km/s, which is why the Moon cannot hold an atmosphere.
questions.hint: Compute \( 2gR \) and take the square root.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \sqrt{gR} \), the orbital velocity, instead of \( \sqrt{2gR} \)
Doubles the correct value, as if the factor 2 were outside the root
Multiplies the orbital velocity by 2 rather than by \( \sqrt2 \)

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: For a satellite in a circular orbit, the ratio of its potential energy to its kinetic energy is
questions.explanation:
\( PE = -\dfrac{G M m}{r} \) and \( KE = \dfrac{G M m}{2r} \).

\( \dfrac{PE}{KE} = \dfrac{-G M m / r}{G M m / 2r} = -2 \).

The potential energy is twice the kinetic energy in magnitude and opposite in sign.
questions.hint: Write both energies with the common factor \( GMm/r \).
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign of the potential energy
Inverts the ratio; potential energy is the larger in magnitude
This is the ratio of total energy to kinetic energy, not of potential to kinetic

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: For a satellite in a circular orbit with kinetic energy \( K \), the total mechanical energy is
questions.explanation:
\( PE = -2K \) for a circular orbit.

\( E = K + PE = K - 2K = -K \).

Also \( E = \dfrac{1}{2} PE \), and the binding energy is \( +K \).
questions.hint: Add the kinetic energy to a potential energy that is \( -2K \).
distractor_logic: Drops the potential energy altogether
This is the potential energy, not the total
Both the sign and the magnitude are wrong; total energy is negative

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: A satellite in a circular orbit has kinetic energy \( 3.2 \times 10^9 \) J. Its total mechanical energy is
questions.explanation:
For a circular orbit \( E = -KE \).

\( E = -3.2 \times 10^9 \) J.

The potential energy is \( -6.4 \times 10^9 \) J, and \( E = KE + PE = 3.2 \times 10^9 - 6.4 \times 10^9 = -3.2 \times 10^9 \) J.
questions.hint: Total energy equals minus the kinetic energy.
distractor_logic: Equates total energy to kinetic energy, ignoring the negative potential energy
This is the potential energy, not the total
Halves the magnitude without justification

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: The orbital velocity of a satellite close to the Earth's surface is 8 km/s. The orbital velocity of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius \( 2R \) (where \( R \) is the Earth's radius) is
questions.explanation:
\( v_o \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt r} \).

Doubling \( r \) divides \( v_o \) by \( \sqrt2 \): \( v = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt2} = 4\sqrt2 \) km/s.
questions.hint: Inverse square root of the radius ratio.
distractor_logic: Divides by 2 instead of by \( \sqrt2 \)
Assumes orbital speed is independent of radius
Multiplies by \( \sqrt2 \) instead of dividing

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: Two satellites move in circular orbits of radii \( r \) and \( 4r \) around the Earth. The ratio of their orbital speeds is
questions.explanation:
\( v_o \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt r} \).

\( \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4r}{r}} = 2 \).

The inner satellite is twice as fast.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the inverse radius ratio.
distractor_logic: Uses \( v \propto 1/r \) instead of \( 1/\sqrt r \)
Inverts the ratio; the inner satellite is faster
This is the period ratio (\( T \propto r^{3/2} \)), not the speed ratio

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: If the mass of a satellite in a given circular orbit were doubled (orbit radius unchanged), its orbital speed would
questions.explanation:
\( v_o = \sqrt{\dfrac{G M}{r}} \) does not contain the satellite's mass.

The speed is unchanged; the kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy each double in magnitude.
questions.hint: Does the satellite's mass appear in the orbital speed formula?
distractor_logic: Confuses the doubling of energies with a doubling of speed
Assumes a heavier satellite must move slower, which the force equation rules out
Applies a square-root scaling to a quantity that has no effect at all

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: The binding energy of a satellite of mass \( m \) in a circular orbit of radius \( r \) (the minimum energy required to remove it to infinity) is
questions.explanation:
Total energy in orbit is \( E = -\dfrac{G M m}{2r} \). To free the satellite its total energy must be raised to zero.

Binding energy \( = 0 - E = +\dfrac{G M m}{2r} \).

It is numerically equal to the total energy but positive, and equals the orbital kinetic energy.
questions.hint: Binding energy is how much you must add to bring the (negative) total energy up to zero.
distractor_logic: This is the total energy itself; binding energy is its negative and must be positive
This is the magnitude of the potential energy, twice too large
This is the potential energy, with the wrong sign and magnitude for binding energy

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \) m, the time period of a satellite in a circular orbit just above the Earth's surface is
questions.explanation:
\( T = \dfrac{2\pi R}{v_o} \) with \( v_o = \sqrt{g R} = 8000 \) m/s.

\( T = \dfrac{2\pi \times 6.4 \times 10^6}{8000} = 1600\pi \) s.

\( 1600\pi \approx 5027 \) s, which is about 84 minutes.
questions.hint: Divide the circumference \( 2\pi R \) by 8 km/s.
distractor_logic: This is the geostationary period, which needs a much larger orbit
Halves the correct value, typically from using \( \pi R \) instead of \( 2\pi R \)
Doubles the correct value

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: A person of mass 50 kg stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s\(^2\). Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\), the scale reads
questions.explanation:
Upward acceleration: \( N - m g = m a \), so \( N = m(g + a) \).

\( N = 50 \times (10 + 2) = 600 \) N.

The apparent weight exceeds the true weight of 500 N.
questions.hint: Add \( ma \) to \( mg \) when the lift accelerates upward.
distractor_logic: Subtracts \( ma \), which is the case for downward acceleration
Ignores the acceleration and gives the true weight
Gives \( ma \) alone, forgetting gravity

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: A person of mass 50 kg stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating downward at 2 m/s\(^2\). Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\), the scale reads
questions.explanation:
Downward acceleration: \( m g - N = m a \), so \( N = m(g - a) \).

\( N = 50 \times (10 - 2) = 400 \) N.
questions.hint: Subtract \( ma \) from \( mg \) when the lift accelerates downward.
distractor_logic: Adds \( ma \), which is the case for upward acceleration
Ignores the acceleration and gives the true weight
Zero reading occurs only for free fall with \( a = g \)

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: A polar satellite has a period of about 100 minutes. The approximate number of revolutions it completes around the Earth in one day is
questions.explanation:
One day has \( 24 \times 60 = 1440 \) minutes.

Number of revolutions \( = \dfrac{1440}{100} \approx 14 \).

During each revolution the Earth turns by about \( 25^\circ \), so successive passes cover new strips of ground.
questions.hint: Divide the minutes in a day by the period.
distractor_logic: One revolution per day is the geostationary case
Assumes a one-hour period
Assumes a period of about 200 minutes

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: Two satellites orbit the Earth in circular orbits with periods in the ratio \( 1 : 8 \). The ratio of their orbital radii is
questions.explanation:
Kepler's third law: \( \dfrac{r_1^3}{r_2^3} = \dfrac{T_1^2}{T_2^2} = \dfrac{1}{64} \).

\( \dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{64}} = \dfrac{1}{4} \).
questions.hint: Square the period ratio, then take the cube root.
distractor_logic: Takes the cube root of the period ratio without squaring first
Assumes the radius ratio equals the period ratio
Reports the ratio of \( r^3 \), not of \( r \)

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: Which type of satellite is best suited for surveying and mapping the entire surface of the Earth over a period of days?
options: a satellite in a low-altitude equatorial orbit
questions.explanation:
A polar satellite passes over both poles in a low orbit while the Earth rotates beneath it.

Each pass photographs a new strip, so in a few days the whole surface is covered.

A geostationary satellite always sees the same region and cannot image the polar areas well.
questions.hint: Which orbit lets the whole globe pass beneath the satellite over time?
distractor_logic: It stays above one spot and never views most of the Earth
It would repeatedly pass over only the equatorial belt
It is far too distant and not in an Earth orbit at all

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: The orbital radius of a geostationary satellite, measured from the Earth's centre, is approximately
questions.explanation:
The geostationary orbital radius is about 42,000 km and the Earth's radius is about 6400 km.

\( \dfrac{42000}{6400} \approx 6.6 \).

The height above the surface is about 5.6 Earth radii; the radius from the centre is one more.
questions.hint: Orbital radius equals the Earth's radius plus the height of 36,000 km.
distractor_logic: This is the height above the surface in Earth radii, not the orbital radius from the centre
Far too small; the period at \( 2R \) is only a few hours
Too large; a period of 24 hours corresponds to about \( 6.6R \)

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: Can a geostationary satellite be placed directly above New Delhi (latitude about \( 28^\circ \) N)?
options: Yes, at a height of 36,000 km directly above the city
Yes, if its speed is increased suitably
No, because a geostationary orbit must lie in the equatorial plane
Yes, with a 24-hour period in any orbital plane
questions.explanation:
Every orbit lies in a plane through the Earth's centre. A satellite hovering above \( 28^\circ \) N would need its orbital plane to be a parallel of latitude, which does not pass through the centre.

A 24-hour orbit in an inclined plane would appear to trace a figure-of-eight in the sky, not stay fixed.

Geostationary satellites exist only above the equator.
questions.hint: An orbital plane must contain the Earth's centre; does a circle of latitude do that?
distractor_logic: Assumes any point can have a satellite hovering above it
Speed cannot change the fact that the orbital plane must pass through the centre
A 24-hour period alone is not enough; the plane must also be equatorial

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: A simple pendulum is set up inside a lift. If the lift's cable snaps and the lift falls freely, the pendulum's time period
options: becomes half of its earlier value
becomes infinite; the pendulum does not oscillate
questions.explanation:
Inside a freely falling lift the effective gravity is \( g - g = 0 \).

\( T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{eff}}} \) with \( g_{eff} = 0 \) gives an infinite period: there is no restoring force, so the bob stays wherever it is placed.
questions.hint: What is the effective gravity inside a freely falling frame?
distractor_logic: Ignores that the effective gravity has changed
Halving would need \( g_{eff} = 4g \)
Zero period would need infinite effective gravity

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: The Earth orbits the Sun in a nearly circular orbit of radius \( 1.5 \times 10^{11} \) m with a period of \( 3.15 \times 10^7 \) s. Taking \( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \) N m\(^2\) kg\(^{-2}\), the mass of the Sun is approximately
questions.explanation:
For a circular orbit, \( \dfrac{G M_s m}{r^2} = m \dfrac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2} \), giving \( M_s = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r^3}{G T^2} \).

\( r^3 = (1.5 \times 10^{11})^3 \approx 3.4 \times 10^{33} \) and \( T^2 \approx 9.9 \times 10^{14} \).

\( M_s \approx \dfrac{39.5 \times 3.4 \times 10^{33}}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 9.9 \times 10^{14}} \approx 2 \times 10^{30} \) kg.
questions.hint: Equate gravitational force to centripetal force, then solve for the central mass.
distractor_logic: This is the order of magnitude of the Earth's mass, not the Sun's
Under-estimates by three orders of magnitude, typically from forgetting the cube on \( r \)
Over-estimates by three orders of magnitude, typically from forgetting the square on \( T \)

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: Suppose the gravitational force between the Sun and a planet varied as \( \dfrac{1}{r^3} \) instead of \( \dfrac{1}{r^2} \). For circular orbits, Kepler's third law would then take the form
questions.explanation:
For a circular orbit the gravitational force supplies the centripetal force: \( \dfrac{k}{r^3} = m \omega^2 r \).

So \( \omega^2 \propto r^{-4} \), and since \( T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} \), we get \( T^2 \propto r^4 \).

In general, an inverse \( r^n \) force gives \( T^2 \propto r^{n+1} \).
questions.hint: Set the hypothetical force equal to \( m \omega^2 r \) and see how \( \omega \) depends on \( r \).
distractor_logic: This is the actual inverse-square result, not the hypothetical inverse-cube one
Adds two to the exponent instead of one
Gives the answer for an inverse-first-power force

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: For circular orbits obeying \( T^2 \propto r^3 \), the orbital speed \( v \) of a planet depends on the orbital radius \( r \) as
questions.explanation:
For a circular orbit \( v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} \).

Since \( T \propto r^{3/2} \), we get \( v \propto \dfrac{r}{r^{3/2}} = r^{-1/2} \).

So outer planets move more slowly, consistent with \( v = \sqrt{\dfrac{G M}{r}} \).
questions.hint: Write \( v = 2\pi r / T \) and substitute how \( T \) scales with \( r \).
distractor_logic: Would follow if \( T \) were proportional to \( r^2 \), which is not Kepler's law
Reverses the sign of the exponent, making outer planets faster
Uses the exponent of \( T \) itself instead of dividing \( r \) by it

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: Planet A has mass \( 2m \) and orbits the Sun at distance \( r \). Planet B has mass \( m \) and orbits at distance \( \dfrac{r}{2} \). The ratio of the gravitational force exerted by the Sun on A to that on B is
questions.explanation:
\( F_A = \dfrac{G M_s (2m)}{r^2} \) and \( F_B = \dfrac{G M_s m}{(r/2)^2} = \dfrac{4 G M_s m}{r^2} \).

\( \dfrac{F_A}{F_B} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2} \).

Halving the distance quadruples the force, which outweighs A's doubled mass.
questions.hint: Doubling the mass doubles the force, but halving the distance quadruples it.
distractor_logic: Considers only the mass factor and ignores the distance difference
Multiplies the mass factor 2 by the distance factor 4 instead of dividing
Inverts the correct ratio

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: A comet moves around the Sun in a highly elongated elliptical orbit. Which of the following quantities remains constant throughout its motion?
options: its angular momentum about the Sun
questions.explanation:
Gravity is a central force directed toward the Sun, so its torque about the Sun is zero and angular momentum is conserved.

Speed and kinetic energy change as the comet moves between perihelion and aphelion.

Linear momentum changes because its direction keeps changing along the curved path.
questions.hint: Which conservation law follows from the force always pointing toward the Sun?
distractor_logic: Kinetic energy is largest at perihelion and smallest at aphelion, so it is not constant
Linear momentum is a vector whose direction turns continuously along the orbit
Speed varies according to Kepler's second law

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: Two point masses of 1 kg and 4 kg are fixed 3 m apart. The point on the line joining them where the net gravitational field is zero is at a distance from the 1 kg mass of
questions.explanation:
Let the point be at distance \( x \) from the 1 kg mass, so it is at \( 3 - x \) from the 4 kg mass.

Setting the fields equal: \( \dfrac{G(1)}{x^2} = \dfrac{G(4)}{(3-x)^2} \), so \( (3 - x) = 2x \).

\( x = 1 \) m. The null point lies closer to the lighter mass.
questions.hint: The null point must be nearer the smaller mass; equate the two field magnitudes.
distractor_logic: Gives the distance from the 4 kg mass instead of from the 1 kg mass
Places the point at the midpoint, ignoring the unequal masses
Solves as though the field varied inversely with distance rather than with its square

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: The value of \( g \) at a small height \( h \) above the Earth's surface equals its value at a depth \( d \) below the surface (both \( h \) and \( d \) much smaller than \( R \)). Then
questions.explanation:
At height: \( g_h \approx g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) \). At depth: \( g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right) \).

Equating the two: \( \dfrac{2h}{R} = \dfrac{d}{R} \).

So \( d = 2h \): you must go twice as deep as you went up to get the same reduction.
questions.hint: Compare the fractional reductions \( 2h/R \) and \( d/R \).
distractor_logic: Assumes the height and depth formulas are identical
Inverts the relation between the two
Squares the factor 2 instead of using it once

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \) m, the angular speed with which the Earth would have to rotate for a body on the equator to become weightless is
questions.explanation:
Weightlessness at the equator requires \( g - R \omega^2 = 0 \), so \( \omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}} \).

\( \dfrac{g}{R} = \dfrac{10}{6.4 \times 10^6} = 1.5625 \times 10^{-6} \).

\( \omega = \sqrt{1.5625 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.25 \times 10^{-3} \) rad/s, about 17 times the present rate.
questions.hint: Set the effective gravity \( g - R\omega^2 \) to zero.
distractor_logic: This is the Earth's actual angular speed, at which bodies are clearly not weightless
Reports \( g/R \) without taking its square root
Doubles the correct value, as if solving \( g = R\omega^2/4 \)

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: A body weighs 90 N on the Earth's surface. Using the exact inverse-square relation, its weight at a height of \( \dfrac{R}{2} \) above the surface is
questions.explanation:
At height \( h = \dfrac{R}{2} \), the distance from the centre is \( \dfrac{3R}{2} \).

\( g_h = g\left(\dfrac{R}{3R/2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}\,g \).

Weight \( = 90 \times \dfrac{4}{9} = 40 \) N. The linear approximation is invalid here since \( h \) is not small compared with \( R \).
questions.hint: Distance from the centre becomes \( 1.5R \); square the ratio.
distractor_logic: Comes from the linear formula \( 1 - 2h/R \) with \( h = R/2 \), which wrongly gives zero
Uses the depth formula \( 1 - d/R \) as if the body were at a depth \( R/2 \)
Uses the ratio \( R/(1.5R) \) without squaring it

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: Treating the Earth as a uniform solid sphere of radius \( R \), which statement correctly describes how the gravitational field \( g \) varies with the distance \( r \) from the centre?
options: \( g \) decreases as \( \dfrac{1}{r^2} \) both inside and outside the Earth
\( g \) increases linearly with \( r \) for \( r < R \) and decreases as \( \dfrac{1}{r^2} \) for \( r > R \)
\( g \) is constant inside the Earth and decreases linearly outside it
\( g \) increases linearly inside and stays constant outside
questions.explanation:
Inside: only the mass within radius \( r \) contributes, giving \( g = \dfrac{G M r}{R^3} \), which is linear in \( r \) and zero at the centre.

Outside: all the mass acts as if concentrated at the centre, giving \( g = \dfrac{G M}{r^2} \).

The two expressions match at \( r = R \), where \( g \) is maximum.
questions.hint: Inside, the attracting mass grows as \( r^3 \) while the distance factor is \( 1/r^2 \).
distractor_logic: Wrongly applies the point-mass inverse-square law inside the Earth, which would make \( g \) infinite at the centre
Swaps the inside and outside behaviours
Claims \( g \) does not fall off outside the Earth, contradicting the inverse-square law

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: At which latitude is the reduction in the effective value of \( g \) due to the Earth's rotation exactly half of the reduction at the equator?
questions.explanation:
Reduction \( = R \omega^2 \cos^2 \lambda \), and at the equator it is \( R \omega^2 \).

For half the equatorial reduction, \( \cos^2 \lambda = \dfrac{1}{2} \), so \( \cos \lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \).

\( \lambda = 45^\circ \).
questions.hint: Solve \( \cos^2 \lambda = 1/2 \).
distractor_logic: Comes from setting \( \cos \lambda = 1/2 \) and forgetting to square, or reading \( 30^\circ \) off as half of \( 60^\circ \)
At \( 60^\circ \) the reduction is one-fourth, not one-half, of the equatorial value
At the poles the reduction is zero

questions.topic: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Variation with Height, Depth, and Latitude
questions.question: A body weighs \( W \) on the Earth's surface. Let \( W_1 \) be its weight at a depth \( \dfrac{R}{4} \) below the surface and \( W_2 \) its weight at a height \( \dfrac{R}{4} \) above the surface (use the exact inverse-square relation for the height). The ratio \( W_1 : W_2 \) is
questions.explanation:
At depth \( \dfrac{R}{4} \): \( W_1 = W\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3}{4}W = 0.75\,W \).

At height \( \dfrac{R}{4} \): distance from centre is \( \dfrac{5R}{4} \), so \( W_2 = W\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^2 = \dfrac{16}{25}W = 0.64\,W \).

\( W_1 : W_2 = 0.75 : 0.64 = 75 : 64 \).
questions.hint: Depth uses the exact linear formula; height uses the exact inverse-square formula.
distractor_logic: Assumes equal displacement from the surface gives equal reduction in either direction
Inverts the ratio; the body is heavier at the depth than at the height
Comes from using the linear approximation \( 1 - 2h/R = 1/2 \) at the height, which is invalid for \( h = R/4 \)

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: A body is projected vertically upward from the Earth's surface with a speed equal to half the escape velocity. Neglecting air resistance, the maximum height it reaches above the surface is
questions.explanation:
Initial KE \( = \dfrac{1}{2} m \left(\dfrac{v_e}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} m v_e^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} m g R \).

Energy conservation: \( \dfrac{1}{4} m g R = \dfrac{m g h R}{R + h} \), so \( \dfrac{h}{R + h} = \dfrac{1}{4} \).

\( 4h = R + h \), giving \( h = \dfrac{R}{3} \).
questions.hint: Kinetic energy is one-fourth of the escape energy; use the exact \( \Delta U \) expression, not \( mgh \).
distractor_logic: Comes from using \( mgh \), which is only valid for \( h \ll R \)
Assumes half the escape speed reaches half the escape height, which has no meaning
This is the height for a launch speed equal to the orbital velocity

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: A body is projected from the Earth's surface with a speed equal to twice the escape velocity. Neglecting air resistance, its speed when it is very far from the Earth is
questions.explanation:
Energy conservation: \( \dfrac{1}{2} m (2 v_e)^2 - \dfrac{G M m}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_{\infty}^2 + 0 \).

Since \( \dfrac{G M m}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_e^2 \), we get \( 4 v_e^2 - v_e^2 = v_{\infty}^2 \).

\( v_{\infty} = \sqrt3\, v_e \).
questions.hint: Write \( v^2 - v_e^2 = v_{\infty}^2 \).
distractor_logic: Subtracts one \( v_e \) from \( 2v_e \) linearly instead of subtracting squares
Comes from \( 4v_e^2 - 2v_e^2 \), doubling the potential energy term
Ignores gravity altogether and adds instead of subtracting

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: A body is projected vertically upward from the Earth's surface with speed \( \sqrt{g R} \). Neglecting air resistance, the maximum height reached above the surface is
questions.explanation:
Initial KE \( = \dfrac{1}{2} m g R \).

Set equal to \( \Delta U = \dfrac{m g h R}{R + h} \): \( \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{h}{R + h} \).

\( R + h = 2h \), so \( h = R \). The body rises to a distance \( 2R \) from the centre.
questions.hint: The launch energy is exactly half the escape energy; use the exact \( \Delta U \).
distractor_logic: Comes from \( \dfrac{1}{2} m g R = m g h \), the small-height approximation
Confuses the final distance from the centre with the height above the surface
This is the height for a launch at half the escape speed

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: The change in gravitational potential energy when a body of mass \( m \) is taken from the Earth's surface to a height \( R \) above it is
questions.explanation:
\( U_{surface} = -\dfrac{G M m}{R} = -m g R \) and \( U_{2R} = -\dfrac{G M m}{2R} = -\dfrac{m g R}{2} \).

\( \Delta U = -\dfrac{m g R}{2} - (-m g R) = +\dfrac{m g R}{2} \).

The potential energy increases (becomes less negative) as the body is raised.
questions.hint: Subtract the surface value from the value at distance \( 2R \).
distractor_logic: Comes from \( mgh \) with \( h = R \), which greatly over-estimates for such a large height
Comes from \( m g h R/(R+h) \) with a slip giving \( R/4 \)
Has the wrong sign; raising a body increases its potential energy

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \) m, the gravitational potential on the Earth's surface (zero at infinity) is
questions.explanation:
\( V = -\dfrac{G M}{R} = -g R \), using \( G M = g R^2 \).

\( V = -10 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 = -6.4 \times 10^7 \) J/kg.

A 100 kg body would therefore have \( U = -6.4 \times 10^9 \) J.
questions.hint: Potential is \( -gR \) at the surface; keep the negative sign.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign
Halves the magnitude, confusing \( gR \) with \( gR/2 \)
This is the potential energy of a 100 kg mass, not the potential per unit mass

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: A planet has the same average density as the Earth but twice its radius. If the escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s, the escape velocity from that planet is
questions.explanation:
\( v_e = \sqrt{2 g R} \) and for fixed density \( g \propto R \), so \( v_e \propto \sqrt{R \cdot R} = R \).

Doubling the radius at the same density doubles the escape velocity.

\( v_e = 2 \times 11.2 = 22.4 \) km/s.
questions.hint: Write \( M \) in terms of density: \( v_e^2 \propto M/R \propto R^2 \).
distractor_logic: Assumes same density means same escape velocity
Uses \( v_e \propto \sqrt{R} \), forgetting that the mass also grows as \( R^3 \)
Uses \( v_e \propto R^2 \) instead of \( R \)

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: The minimum energy required to launch a satellite of mass \( m \) from the Earth's surface into a circular orbit of radius \( 2R \) (\( R \) = Earth's radius, \( g \) = surface gravity) is
questions.explanation:
Energy at the surface (at rest): \( E_1 = -\dfrac{G M m}{R} = -m g R \).

Energy in orbit at \( 2R \): \( E_2 = -\dfrac{G M m}{2(2R)} = -\dfrac{m g R}{4} \).

Required energy \( = E_2 - E_1 = -\dfrac{m g R}{4} + m g R = \dfrac{3}{4} m g R \).
questions.hint: Subtract the surface energy (potential only) from the orbital total energy.
distractor_logic: This is only the magnitude of the orbital total energy, not the change from the surface
Accounts only for the change in potential energy and forgets the orbital kinetic energy
This is the energy to escape entirely, more than an orbit at \( 2R \) needs

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \) m, the total mechanical energy of a 100 kg satellite in a circular orbit of radius \( 2R \) is
questions.explanation:
\( E = -\dfrac{G M m}{2r} = -\dfrac{m g R^2}{2(2R)} = -\dfrac{m g R}{4} \).

\( E = -\dfrac{100 \times 10 \times 6.4 \times 10^6}{4} = -1.6 \times 10^9 \) J.
questions.hint: Total energy is \( -GMm/2r \) with \( r = 2R \) and \( GM = gR^2 \).
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign; a positive total energy means the satellite is not bound
This is the potential energy at \( 2R \), twice the magnitude of the total energy
This is the potential energy at the surface, not in the orbit

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: A satellite is moving in a circular orbit around the Earth. If its speed is suddenly increased to \( \sqrt2 \) times its orbital speed (direction unchanged), the satellite will
options: escape from the Earth's gravitational field
move into a larger circular orbit
continue in the same orbit with twice the period
questions.explanation:
At any radius \( r \), the escape speed is \( \sqrt{\dfrac{2 G M}{r}} = \sqrt2\,v_o \).

Increasing the speed to \( \sqrt2\,v_o \) makes the total energy exactly zero, so the satellite follows an open (parabolic) path and escapes.
questions.hint: Compare the new speed with the escape speed at that radius.
distractor_logic: A larger circular orbit needs a specific smaller speed at the larger radius, not just a higher speed here
Increasing the speed takes the satellite outward, not inward
The orbit changes completely; it does not remain circular

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: Two satellites of the same mass move in circular orbits of radii \( r \) and \( 2r \). The ratio of the kinetic energy of the inner satellite to that of the outer one is
questions.explanation:
\( KE = \dfrac{G M m}{2r} \), so \( KE \propto \dfrac{1}{r} \).

\( \dfrac{KE_1}{KE_2} = \dfrac{2r}{r} = 2 \).

The inner satellite has twice the kinetic energy (and \( \sqrt2 \) times the speed).
questions.hint: Kinetic energy goes as \( 1/r \), speed as \( 1/\sqrt r \).
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio; the inner satellite is faster
Uses \( KE \propto 1/r^2 \) as if kinetic energy followed the force law
This is the ratio of speeds, not of kinetic energies

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: A satellite in a low circular orbit gradually loses mechanical energy because of friction with the thin upper atmosphere. As a result, its orbital speed
options: decreases, along with its total energy
increases, even though its total energy decreases
becomes zero and the satellite stops
questions.explanation:
Losing total energy makes \( E = -\dfrac{G M m}{2r} \) more negative, which requires a smaller \( r \).

At a smaller radius the orbital speed \( \sqrt{\dfrac{G M}{r}} \) is larger.

The satellite spirals inward and speeds up: the lost potential energy exceeds the energy lost to friction.
questions.hint: Which way does \( r \) change when \( E \) becomes more negative, and how does \( v_o \) depend on \( r \)?
distractor_logic: Assumes losing energy must mean losing speed, ignoring that \( KE = -E \) grows as \( E \) falls
The orbit shrinks, so the speed must change
Friction shrinks the orbit rather than stopping the satellite in place

questions.topic: Orbital Motion of Satellites: Orbital Velocity, Time Period, and Total Energy
questions.question: The additional energy required to shift a satellite of mass \( m \) from a circular orbit of radius \( r \) to a circular orbit of radius \( 2r \) around the Earth (mass \( M \)) is
questions.explanation:
\( E_1 = -\dfrac{G M m}{2r} \) and \( E_2 = -\dfrac{G M m}{4r} \).

\( \Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = -\dfrac{G M m}{4r} + \dfrac{G M m}{2r} = \dfrac{G M m}{4r} \).

The higher orbit has a less negative total energy, so energy must be supplied.
questions.hint: Subtract the two total energies \( -GMm/2r \) and \( -GMm/4r \).
distractor_logic: Uses the change in potential energy alone and ignores the change in kinetic energy
Wrong sign; moving outward requires energy to be added
This is the energy to go from the surface to orbit \( 2R \), a different problem

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: A geostationary satellite orbits at a radius of 42,000 km with a period of 24 hours. The orbital radius of a satellite with a period of 3 hours is
questions.explanation:
Period ratio \( = \dfrac{3}{24} = \dfrac{1}{8} \).

Kepler's third law: \( \dfrac{r^3}{r_g^3} = \left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{64} \), so \( \dfrac{r}{r_g} = \dfrac{1}{4} \).

\( r = \dfrac{42000}{4} = 10500 \) km.
questions.hint: Square the period ratio, then take the cube root.
distractor_logic: Takes the cube root of the period ratio without squaring it
Assumes radius is proportional to period
Goes the wrong way; a shorter period needs a smaller orbit

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: A geostationary satellite orbits at a radius of about \( 4.2 \times 10^7 \) m with a period of 24 hours. Its orbital speed is approximately
questions.explanation:
\( v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 4.2 \times 10^7}{86400} \) m/s.

\( v \approx \dfrac{2.64 \times 10^8}{8.64 \times 10^4} \approx 3.1 \times 10^3 \) m/s, about 3 km/s.

This is much slower than the 8 km/s of a low-orbit satellite, as expected for a larger radius.
questions.hint: Speed is circumference divided by period; convert 24 hours to seconds.
distractor_logic: This is the low-orbit speed near the surface, not at 6.6 Earth radii
This is the escape velocity from the surface
Too small by a factor of about 6; check the arithmetic on \( 2\pi r/T \)

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: An astronaut of mass 70 kg is in a satellite in a circular orbit of radius \( 2R \) (\( R \) = Earth's radius). Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\) at the surface, the actual gravitational force on the astronaut and the apparent weight he experiences are, respectively,
questions.explanation:
At distance \( 2R \), \( g' = \dfrac{g}{4} = 2.5 \) m/s\(^2\), so the true gravitational force is \( 70 \times 2.5 = 175 \) N.

The astronaut is in free fall along with the satellite, so the normal reaction and hence the apparent weight is zero.

Weightlessness does not mean the absence of gravity.
questions.hint: Gravity still acts (inverse-square), but the floor pushes back with nothing.
distractor_logic: Assumes gravity vanishes in orbit; it is what keeps the satellite moving in a circle
Uses the surface value of \( g \) at a distance of \( 2R \) from the centre
Uses \( g/2 \) and forgets that the astronaut is in free fall

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: A person's apparent weight in a lift is 1.5 times his true weight. Taking \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\), the lift is accelerating
questions.explanation:
\( N = m(g + a) = 1.5\, m g \).

\( g + a = 15 \), so \( a = 5 \) m/s\(^2\) upward.

A downward acceleration would reduce the apparent weight below the true weight.
questions.hint: Set \( m(g+a) = 1.5\,mg \) and solve for \( a \).
distractor_logic: Would give an apparent weight of \( 2mg \)
Would give an apparent weight of \( 2.5mg \)
Downward acceleration makes the reading smaller, not larger

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: A satellite orbits a planet in a circular orbit of radius \( r \) with period \( T \). If the planet's mass were four times as large while the orbital radius stayed the same, the new period would be
questions.explanation:
\( T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{G M}} \), so \( T \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt M} \) for fixed \( r \).

Four times the mass gives \( \dfrac{T}{\sqrt4} = \dfrac{T}{2} \).

A more massive planet pulls harder, so the satellite must move faster to stay in the same orbit.
questions.hint: Kepler's third law contains the central mass in the denominator, under a square root.
distractor_logic: Reverses the trend; stronger gravity means a faster orbit
Uses \( T \propto 1/M \) instead of \( 1/\sqrt M \)
Assumes the period depends on the radius alone

questions.topic: Geostationary and Polar Satellites, Weightlessness, and Kepler's Third Law Applications
questions.question: A polar satellite can photograph the entire surface of the Earth over a few days because
options: its orbital plane rotates along with the Earth
its orbital plane stays fixed in space while the Earth rotates beneath it
it has a period of 24 hours
it remains stationary above the pole
questions.explanation:
The orbital plane of a polar satellite is essentially fixed in space and passes over both poles.

As the Earth rotates about its axis, a different strip of the surface lies beneath the satellite on each successive pass (about 14 per day).

Over a few days these strips cover the whole globe.
questions.hint: Think about which of the two, the satellite's plane or the ground, is doing the turning.
distractor_logic: If the plane rotated with the Earth the satellite would see the same strip repeatedly
Its period is about 100 minutes, not 24 hours
No satellite can hover above a pole

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: A satellite in a circular orbit has gravitational potential energy \( -8 \times 10^9 \) J. Its total mechanical energy is
questions.explanation:
For a circular orbit \( E = \dfrac{1}{2} PE \).

\( E = \dfrac{1}{2}(-8 \times 10^9) = -4 \times 10^9 \) J.

The kinetic energy is \( +4 \times 10^9 \) J, and \( KE + PE = -4 \times 10^9 \) J.
questions.hint: Total energy is half the potential energy, keeping its negative sign.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign; a bound orbit has negative total energy
Equates total energy to potential energy, forgetting the positive kinetic energy
Doubles the potential energy instead of halving it

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: The orbital velocity just above the Earth's surface is 8 km/s. The escape velocity for a body located at a height \( R \) above the surface (\( R \) = Earth's radius) is
questions.explanation:
At distance \( 2R \) from the centre, \( v_e' = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 G M}{2R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{G M}{R}} \).

This equals the surface orbital velocity, 8 km/s.

The orbital velocity at \( 2R \) is \( 4\sqrt2 \) km/s, and \( 8 = \sqrt2 \times 4\sqrt2 \), so the \( \sqrt2 \) ratio still holds at that radius.
questions.hint: Halving the \( GM/r \) term under the root exactly cancels the factor 2 of escape.
distractor_logic: This is the escape velocity from the surface, not from height \( R \)
This is the orbital velocity at \( 2R \), which is smaller than the escape velocity there by \( \sqrt2 \)
Doubles the surface orbital velocity for no reason

questions.question: A planet has surface gravity \( g = 5 \) m/s\(^2\) and radius \( 3.2 \times 10^6 \) m. The orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit just above its surface is
questions.explanation:
\( v_o = \sqrt{g R} = \sqrt{5 \times 3.2 \times 10^6} = \sqrt{1.6 \times 10^7} \) m/s.

\( v_o = 4 \times 10^3 \) m/s \( = 4 \) km/s.

Both \( g \) and \( R \) are half the Earth's values, so \( gR \) is one-fourth and \( v_o \) is half of 8 km/s.
questions.hint: Use \( v_o = \sqrt{gR} \) with the planet's own values.
distractor_logic: This is the Earth's value; both \( g \) and \( R \) are smaller here

questions.topic: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
questions.question: A satellite of mass \( m \) in a circular orbit of radius \( r \) has total energy \( E \) (negative). It is moved to a circular orbit of radius \( 4r \). Its new total energy and new period, compared with the old ones, are
questions.explanation:
Total energy \( E = -\dfrac{G M m}{2r} \propto \dfrac{1}{r} \), so at \( 4r \) it becomes \( \dfrac{E}{4} \) (less negative).

Kepler's third law: \( T \propto r^{3/2} \), so the period becomes \( 4^{3/2} = 8 \) times.
questions.hint: Energy magnitude scales as \( 1/r \), period as \( r^{3/2} \).
distractor_logic: Makes the energy more negative at a larger radius, the wrong direction
Uses \( E \propto 1/\sqrt r \) and \( T \propto r \)

questions.question: A planet has the same radius as the Earth but one-fourth of its mass. If the escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s, the surface gravity ratio (planet to Earth) and the escape velocity from the planet are, respectively,
questions.explanation:

\( v_e = \sqrt{2 g R} \propto \sqrt g \), so \( v_e = \dfrac{11.2}{\sqrt4} = 5.6 \) km/s.
questions.hint: \( g \) scales with the mass; \( v_e \) scales with the square root of \( g \).

questions.question: The time period of a satellite in a circular orbit just above the surface of a planet with surface gravity \( g \) and radius \( R \) is
questions.explanation:
\( T = \dfrac{2\pi R}{v_o} \) with \( v_o = \sqrt{g R} \).

\( T = \dfrac{2\pi R}{\sqrt{g R}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}} \).

This is the same form as a simple pendulum of length \( R \).

Dimensionally a time squared, from forgetting the square root

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: An astronaut in a geostationary satellite is weightless. Which statement about her is correct?
options: Her gravitational potential energy is negative and her apparent weight is zero
Her gravitational potential energy is zero because gravity does not act on her
Her gravitational potential energy is positive because she is very high up
Her apparent weight equals her surface weight because the satellite is stationary
questions.explanation:
At an orbital radius of about 42,000 km she is still well within the Earth's gravitational field, and her potential energy \( -\dfrac{G M m}{r} \) is negative.

She is in free fall along with the satellite, so the normal reaction and hence the apparent weight is zero.

A geostationary satellite is stationary only relative to the ground, not in space.
questions.hint: Weightlessness is about the missing normal force, not the absence of gravity.
distractor_logic: Gravity acts strongly at that radius; potential energy is zero only at infinity
Potential energy with the zero at infinity is negative at every finite distance
Stationary relative to the ground does not remove the free-fall condition

questions.topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
questions.question: For a satellite of given mass, the energy required to make it escape the Earth's gravity from a geostationary orbit, compared with that from a low orbit close to the surface, is
options: larger, because the satellite is farther from the Earth
smaller, because the binding energy \( \dfrac{G M m}{2r} \) decreases with \( r \)
the same, because escape energy does not depend on the orbit
zero, because a geostationary satellite is already free of the Earth's gravity
questions.explanation:
The binding energy of a circular orbit is \( \dfrac{G M m}{2r} \).

The geostationary radius is about 6.6 times the low-orbit radius, so its binding energy is about one-sixth as large.

Less energy is needed to escape from the higher orbit, because the satellite is already less tightly bound.
questions.hint: Binding energy falls as \( 1/r \).
distractor_logic: Being farther away means being less bound, not more
Escape energy from an orbit depends on the orbital radius
The satellite is still bound; its total energy is negative

questions.question: A satellite in a circular orbit has kinetic energy \( K \). The minimum additional kinetic energy that must be given to it (in the direction of motion) so that it just escapes from the Earth is
questions.explanation:
Escape from radius \( r \) needs speed \( \sqrt2\,v_o \), i.e. kinetic energy \( 2K \).

The satellite already has \( K \), so the extra needed is \( 2K - K = K \).

Equivalently, its total energy \( -K \) must be raised to zero.

Kepler's third law: \( \dfrac{r_g}{R} = (17.1)^{2/3} \approx 6.6 \).

So the geostationary orbit has a radius of about 6.6 Earth radii, i.e. about 42,000 km.
